subject: Climate & Environment
title: What 1.5°C Means for the World
description: A micro-lesson that makes What 1.5°C Means for the World usable.

hook.text: Half a degree sounds trivial. The jump from 1.5°C to 2°C of warming is enormous.

buildup.text: At 1.5°C, 70% of coral reefs die. At 2°C, virtually all of them vanish.

discovery.text: At 1.5°C, 14% of people face severe heat. At 2°C, that number jumps to 37%.

twist.text: We have already warmed 1.1°C. The window to stay below 1.5°C closes around 2030.

climax.text: Every fraction of a degree we prevent saves lives, species, and coastlines.

punchline.text: Half a degree is the gap between hard and catastrophic.

quiz.question: What happens to coral reefs at 2°C of warming?

details.summary: The 1.5-degree Celsius warming limit, enshrined in the Paris Agreement, represents the threshold beyond which coral reefs die en masse, extreme heat becomes routine, and vulnerable nations face existential threats. Even half a degree more to 2 degrees sharply increases risks across every sector.
details.whyItMatters: The difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees is not gradual — it is the difference between manageable and catastrophic for many ecosystems and communities.
takeaways: At 1.5 degrees, 70 to 90 percent of coral reefs die; at 2 degrees, over 99 percent
Ten million more people face coastal flooding at 2 degrees versus 1.5
Food production decline, water stress, and species loss all jump significantly

faq.question: Is it still possible to limit warming to 1.5 degrees?
faq.answer: Technically possible but extremely challenging. Global emissions would need to fall roughly 45 percent by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050. Current policies put the world on track for 2.5 to 3 degrees by 2100.

faq.question: Why did the Paris Agreement choose 1.5 degrees as a goal?
faq.answer: Small island nations successfully argued that 2 degrees would destroy their countries through sea-level rise. Scientific evidence showed 1.5 degrees dramatically reduces risks to coral reefs, food supplies, and vulnerable populations.
